"Real Hacking
Based on actual UNIX commands, Hacknet focuses on real hacking, not the Hollywood-style version of it. This creates a truly immersive experience and puts players right in the thick of trying to break through the firewalls."

Blatant lies. Hacknet is straight up Hollywood hacking. The terminal is a simplistic cross-breed between bash and cmd.exe. It puts you in the role of a script kiddy, who "hacks" systems by observing which ports are open on the target machine and running the corresponding hacking program by typing its name and a port number (e.g. "FTPHack 21"). Once you're in, your job is to either snoop through some files for a password, to download files, or to delete them using basic terminal skills. You're supposed to cover your tracks by deleting logs, but it rarely matters. The same thing, over and over, no brains required. There's no sense you're accomplishing anything of value, nor of any consequence to yourself or others.

It's an insult to anyone with more than a surface-level understanding of network security, as challenging to a puzzle gamer as 50 consecutive games of Tic-tac-toe, and isn't even that interesting in terms of Hollywood hacking simulations. It's on par with a budding game developer's first project, not something worth spending $10 to $24 on. If you want an intellectual challenge (Hollywood setting, but real problem-solving), check out Zachtronics (Exapunks, Shenzhen I/O, TIS-100).

That said, Hacknet does have a few high points. The music is pretty great. The Labyrinths DLC is slightly less mediocre, but isn't worth the regular $7 price point on top of the base game's $10. If everything was like the DLC's final mission — which unexpectedly drops you into a timed, high-stakes situation with dire consequences — this might actually be a decent game. As is, though, it's just a bland waste of money.

I have nearly 100% the game apart from a few achievements that I didn't get in my first playthrough (although I'll likely have soon if you're reading this in the future) and I'm going to tell you why I believe you should buy Hacknet. When I first bought Hacknet I wasn't really expected much, I mean it's just a clicking and typing game.. right? Well yes you do have the option to use a GUI to click, and primarily type out commands, however it surprised me how well made the game actually is. If you have never used a Linux system before, or Powershell on Windows, this game can actually teach you the basics as you move along in the game. It won't teach you how to actually hack or anything but it will teach you about basic commands used in Linux systems to this day. 

The game has a unique story with questionable morals for that matter. The rough of it is that a professional hacker has entrusted you with some very private information and teaches you the basics of hacking, then promptly disappears without much of a trace. As a hacker you complete contracts for different hacking scene groups and work your way up the hacking group ladders. It all has a climax too, and loads of unique easter eggs and secrets. 

The game does feature some bugs and annoyances, such as the clicking GUI sometimes seemingly not working or taking forever to actually process. But outside of that, it's a really well polished game. I wish I could buy it again for full price.

What a fun way to learn UNIX! This simple text based game is brilliant! It teaches you UNIX from the ground up (seriously, I was a total noob and now I feel fairly fluent in all the commands and functions)! 

The difficulty feels like a natural learning curve and the game play doesn't hold your hand (tho there are three pages of helpful tips you can access at any time via a command prompt, should you need a refresher, as well as terminals dedicated to learning about each executable). And you can figure out best use case and strategies on your own and feel like you're actually a competent user of the UNIX system. Plenty of fun challenges and easter eggs along the way too! Explore!

I can't help but find flaws in its guitar-hero style approach to cyber security.

This game is at its strongest when it closest resembles real hacking: problem solving through enumeration, weaponization and exploitation. This is especially evident when you are plundering compromised hard drives and linking information together to achieve a goal.

The game is at its weakest when it relies too much on the "hacking tools". It's like a less comprehensive version of Metasploit and Nmap where you just use the same modules over and over again. For me, it got boring fast and I would constantly try to rush through the repetition.

Props to whole game being playable from the CLI though.

Solid game, but if you want to do real hacking, go to TryHackMe or HackTheBox.

8/10

EDIT: I have had a couple people contact me, thank you for doing so. I didn't mean to sound cynical, the developer took on a huge challenge and he largely succeeded. Development is really tough.

He got pretty much everything right about the industry however. And there is a balance between real hacking and accessibility being juggled here. When I say, it's the "guitar hero" of hacking, I mean that while the hacks being pulled off are completely plausible in real life, the execution is much, much harder.

It's a video game, so I should have allowed it more grace. If you have a passing interest in hacking, I'd absolutely recommend this game. If you want to do the real deal, feel free to contact me and we can set up some CTFs.

Oh and one more thing: the game's soundtrack is super fun to listen to while doing the real thing. (:

Play Hacknet and learn how to hack into highly secure systems, become a master hacker, and probably get yourself on some kind of government watchlist in the process.

I'm really not sure how this got onto my library, but man am I ever not a fan of it.  

Game seems quite repetitive while also not being particularly engaging to someone with the vaguest understanding of programming and, based on other reviews, is quite frustrating for those who're very experienced with it - leaving it to be enjoyed by only those with a modicum of codemonkey skill under their belt, but not too much.

The game's unique mechanics and addictive storyline make it an absolute pleasure to play.

One of the things I love most about Hacknet is how immersive it is. The game does an incredible job of making you feel like a real hacker with its realistic interface and authentic hacking commands. It's a game that not only entertains but also educates on the intricacies of hacking.

The gameplay itself is challenging but rewarding. Each mission requires careful planning and execution, forcing you to think outside the box to achieve your goals. And the game never feels too difficult, thanks to its clever hint system that guides you in the right direction without giving away the answer entirely.

But what really sets Hacknet apart is its history. The game tells a compelling narrative that will keep you hooked from start to finish. The characters are well developed and the plot twists are brilliant. By the end of the game I was emotionally involved in the outcome of the story.

Overall, Hacknet is an excellent game that I would recommend to anyone who loves hacking or puzzle games. It offers a unique and immersive experience not to be missed.
